title: Fournier’s gangrene: a review of predictive scoring systems and practical guide for patient management
condition_or_topic: Fournier’s gangrene (FG) and its clinical management and predictive scoring systems
clinical_background: FG is a rare, rapidly spreading necrotising infection of the external genitalia, perineum or perianal region. It occurs predominantly in men and can progress to life-threatening sepsis. Reported risk factors include diabetes mellitus, alcohol excess, lower socioeconomic status, immunocompromised status and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection. Historically, mortality has been estimated at 15–40%; a more recent meta-analysis reported a mean mortality of 7.3%. Management requires prompt resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics and surgical removal of necrotic tissue, often followed by further procedures and wound reconstruction. Evidence on long-term outcomes after discharge is limited.
objectives: Provide a practical guide to managing patients with FG.
Review the predictive scoring systems available to assist clinicians caring for patients with FG.
interpretation: Fournier’s gangrene remains a life-threatening condition despite improvement in mortality from historical levels. The authors present care as a sequence of resuscitation, urgent debridement, inpatient antimicrobial and wound management, reconstruction, and long-term follow-up. Each stage requires multidisciplinary expertise. Although several prognostic scores are available, the authors find no clear consensus on whether they should guide care or which score should be preferred. Decisions about faecal diversion, orchidectomy, and adjunctive treatment are individualised.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: Historically reported mortality of 15–40% contrasts with a mean mortality of 7.3% in a recent meta-analysis. Studies cited by the authors have repeatedly validated Fournier’s Gangrene Severity Index (FGSI) as a mortality predictor. The original Uludag Fournier’s Gangrene Severity Index (UFGSI) study reported a 94% probability of death with a score >9 and an 81% probability of survival with a score ⩽9, compared with 75% and 78%, respectively, for FGSI; external studies have also validated UFGSI. A prospective cohort found Charlson Comorbidity Index and Surgical Apgar Score comparable to the FG-specific indices for outcome prediction, while subsequent evidence described Simplified Fournier’s Gangrene Severity Index as non-inferior to FGSI and UFGSI. Evidence cited for vacuum-assisted closure (VAC) therapy suggests better wound closure at a 10-week post-operative interval but does not establish a mortality benefit. Some studies suggest lower mortality with adjunctive hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT), whereas European Association of Urology (EAU) guidelines advise against its use outside clinical trials because the existing evidence is of low quality.
clinical_implications: A clinical diagnosis of Fournier’s gangrene warrants urgent treatment; imaging should not postpone debridement when the disease is clinically obvious or extensive.

Prognostic scores may help estimate outcomes, but their role in treatment decisions remains uncertain. A predicted high risk of death has not been established as a reason to withhold aggressive resuscitation or debridement.
Blood cultures are rarely positive, but positivity is associated with poorer outcomes; wound and debrided-tissue cultures are particularly useful for directing antimicrobial treatment.
Survivors may have persistent physical, sexual, urinary, faecal, and psychological difficulties, so needs after discharge vary with the treatments received.
practice_implications: Begin assessment and resuscitation promptly, give broad-spectrum antibiotics as soon as possible, and obtain cultures first when doing so will not substantially delay antibiotics. Use local antimicrobial guidance and revise treatment in light of culture results.

Arrange extensive surgical debridement as soon as possible after initial resuscitation. Lin et al. identified 14h as the optimal interval for initial debridement and associated longer delays with increased mortality.

Consider urinary or faecal diversion when wound contamination is a risk. Consider faecal diversion for perianal or anal sphincter involvement or faecal incontinence; if a stoma is indicated, fit it during the initial debridement when possible.
Seek plastic-surgery input for definitive wound closure and tailor reconstruction to the individual defect rather than applying a standard technique.

Individualise follow-up to the patient’s operations and post-discharge needs, including physical and psychological needs. After diverting colostomy, arrange stoma-nursing input and colorectal outpatient review to discuss possible reversal.

The article recommends considering intermittent hyperbaric oxygen therapy with multiparameter diagnostic monitoring as post-discharge rehabilitation, while separately noting that EAU guidelines advise against HBOT outside clinical trials because the evidence is of low quality.
limitations: The evidence does not establish a consensus on whether prognostic scoring systems improve management or which system should be used.
No published study has assessed Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotizing Fasciitis (LRINEC) specifically as a diagnostic tool for Fournier’s gangrene.
No large-scale randomised trial has compared VAC therapy with simple wound closure, limiting conclusions about VAC therapy.
The cited study of a pedicled gracilis muscle flap for reducing dead space was small (n =22) and retrospective.
The evidence supporting HBOT is of low quality, as noted in the discussion of EAU guidance.
Long-term post-discharge outcomes are poorly documented, and little guidance exists for standardised long-term care and follow-up.
open_questions: Whether prognostic scores should routinely be used in Fournier’s gangrene and, if so, which score is preferable.
Whether a score predicting high mortality should affect decisions to provide aggressive resuscitation and debridement.
Whether neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) should routinely be used to predict outcomes in Fournier’s gangrene.
How care can best be individualised and how survivors’ quality of life can be improved after discharge.
future_directions: Investigate the routine prognostic role of NLR in Fournier’s gangrene.
Conduct larger studies comparing VAC therapy with simple wound closure.
Further investigate reconstruction that reduces anatomical dead space, including the approach assessed in the small retrospective pedicled gracilis muscle flap study.
Study long-term outcomes, individualised follow-up, and quality-of-life measures after discharge.
study_design: Non-systematic literature review using PubMed to examine contemporary management of Fournier’s gangrene (FG), including pathogenesis, risk factors, treatments, reconstruction, outcomes, follow-up, and the utility of scoring systems. Searches used ‘Fournier’, ‘gangrene’, ‘management’, ‘treatment’, ‘reconstruction’, ‘outcomes’, ‘antibiotic’, and ‘microorganism’; ‘scoring’, ‘system’, and ‘index’ were combined with those terms to examine scoring systems.

population.description: Patients with Fournier’s gangrene (FG) discussed in the reviewed literature; no patient cohort was directly enrolled.

main_findings.description: Historical estimates placed mortality from Fournier’s gangrene at 15–40%. A more recent meta-analysis reported lower mean mortality.
main_findings.context: 15–40% is the historical estimate; 7.3% is the mean reported by the cited meta-analysis.

main_findings.description: In the original study by Wong et al., a Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotizing Fasciitis (LRINEC) threshold of six points yielded the reported predictive values for necrotising fasciitis.
main_findings.metric: positive predictive value; negative predictive value
main_findings.context: Both values refer to a cut-off of six points in the cited diagnostic study, not specifically to Fournier’s gangrene.

main_findings.description: A cited meta-analysis found limited sensitivity of Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotizing Fasciitis (LRINEC) for detecting necrotising fasciitis.
main_findings.context: The meta-analysis included 23 studies. Sensitivity was 68.2% at an LRINEC score of ⩾6 and 40.8% at an LRINEC score of ⩾8; these were not results specific to Fournier’s gangrene.

main_findings.description: Laor et al. developed Fournier’s Gangrene Severity Index (FGSI) as a predictor of mortality. The original authors reported the listed probabilities at its proposed cut-off.
main_findings.metric: cut-off value; probability of death; probability of survival
main_findings.context: The cited derivation study included 30 patients with Fournier’s gangrene. The probabilities come from the original authors as presented in Table 1.

main_findings.description: In the analysis used to develop Fournier’s Gangrene Severity Index (FGSI), affected body-surface area and the number of debridement operations did not significantly predict mortality.
main_findings.context: Finding attributed to Laor et al.; neither variable was incorporated into FGSI.

main_findings.description: Yilmazlar et al. identified disease spread and patient age as significant mortality predictors and incorporated them into Uludag Fournier’s Gangrene Severity Index (UFGSI).
main_findings.context: The cited case series included 80 patients and used logistic regression.

main_findings.description: The original Uludag Fournier’s Gangrene Severity Index (UFGSI) study reported the stated probability of death above its threshold and probability of survival at or below it.
main_findings.metric: probability of death; probability of survival
main_findings.context: In Yilmazlar et al., death probability was 94% with UFGSI >9, whereas survival probability was 81% with UFGSI ⩽9. Table 1 gives a cut-off value of 9 and the corresponding 94% and 81% probabilities.

main_findings.description: A cited comparison suggested that Uludag Fournier’s Gangrene Severity Index (UFGSI) was more sensitive but less specific than Fournier’s Gangrene Severity Index (FGSI).
main_findings.context: For sensitivity and specificity, respectively, the first value is UFGSI and the second is FGSI; the review presents this as a suggestion from a cited study.

main_findings.description: A cited prospective cohort found that Charlson Comorbidity Index and Surgical Apgar Score predicted outcomes as well as the Fournier’s gangrene indices.
main_findings.context: Roghmann et al. also considered these tools easier to calculate, more broadly applicable and better validated. Surgical Apgar Score uses intraoperative measurements, limiting its likely preoperative utility.

main_findings.description: Simplified Fournier’s Gangrene Severity Index (SFGSI) was reported to be non-inferior to the previously available FGSI and UFGSI.
main_findings.context: The index uses serum creatinine, haematocrit and serum potassium; Table 1 lists a cut-off value of 2 but no probabilities of death or survival.

main_findings.description: The neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) has been reported to predict intensive care admission, need for mechanical ventilation and mortality in patients with Fournier’s gangrene.
main_findings.context: The authors state that further research is needed before establishing its routine use for outcome prediction in Fournier’s gangrene.

main_findings.description: A cited study associated delaying initial surgical debridement beyond its identified optimal period with increased mortality.
main_findings.context: Finding attributed to Lin et al.; the association concerns delays longer than 14h.

main_findings.description: A cited meta-analysis reported the proportion of patients with Fournier’s gangrene requiring support for at least one organ system, such as mechanical ventilation or dialysis.
main_findings.metric: proportion requiring at least single-system support
main_findings.context: The support requirement relates to postoperative high-dependency care.

main_findings.description: A cited analysis reported that orchidectomy and penectomy were uncommon in the management of Fournier’s gangrene.
main_findings.context: The respective values are for orchidectomy and penectomy.

main_findings.description: Evidence cited by the authors suggests that vacuumassisted closure (VAC) therapy may improve postoperative wound closure, but does not clearly establish a mortality benefit.
main_findings.context: The suggested closure benefit was assessed at a 10-week post-operative interval. The authors note the absence of a large-scale randomised comparison with simple wound closure and limit the strength of the conclusion.

main_findings.description: In a cited retrospective comparison, patients receiving a pedicled gracilis muscle flap to fill dead space had significantly fewer revision operations for wound dehiscence and a significantly shorter hospital stay than those without a specific dead-space procedure.
main_findings.context: The study by Ismayilzade et al. was small (n =22); the review provides no effect size or p value.

main_findings.description: Evidence cited in the review suggests that hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT), added to debridement and antibiotics, significantly reduces mortality.
main_findings.context: The authors note that use depends on available facilities and expertise. They also report that European Association of Urology (EAU) guidelines advise against HBOT outside clinical trials because the existing evidence is of low quality.

notable_adverse_events: Scrotal advancement flaps can fail or develop wound necrosis; the review describes a greater risk of flap failure when used for larger scrotal defects.
Recognised complications of split-thickness skin grafting and thigh flaps include graft loss, infection, scarring, adhesions, dehiscence, unacceptable cosmetic results and reduced sensation.

secondary_results: In Eke’s review of over 1700 cases, sepsis originated from the anorectum in 30–50%, the urogenitalia in 20–40% and genital skin in 20%. Colorectal sources were associated with a worse prognosis.

Diabetes mellitus was described as the most frequent comorbidity among patients with Fournier’s gangrene (30–40%) and as associated with increased mortality. Outcomes were reported to vary with the degree of hyperglycaemia.

Huayllani et al. reported hypertension in 26%, anaemia in 10%, heart failure in 6% and obesity in 12% of patients with Fournier’s gangrene. The review says the effect of these comorbidities on outcomes remains controversial.
Multivariate analyses in cited large studies identified patient age, renal failure, coagulopathy and congestive heart failure as significant mortality risk factors.

Becerra et al. found multiple bacteria in 86% of cases in a study of 131 patients; 55% had Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria in the same culture. Candida was present in 24% of their dataset, compared with 1–5% in similar studies at other institutions.

Blood cultures were described as rarely positive in Fournier’s gangrene, but a positive result was associated with poorer outcomes. Wound cultures were described as the most useful for guiding antibiotics.

The review states that urinary diversion by urethral catheter does not appear to affect mortality. It also cites an association between placing an indicated stoma during the initial debridement, when possible, and better mortality outcomes.
VAC therapy was associated with fewer dressing changes, better pain control and greater mobility; improved mortality rates were not clearly established.
At discharge, Sorensen found that 23% of patients required ‘home health care’ and 6% required a ‘skilled nursing facility’.
The review reports that sepsis develops in over 40% of patients with Fournier’s gangrene and relates this to high 1- and 5-year mortality, without giving those mortality rates.

tables.summary: The table contrasts FG-specific indices with broader prognostic tools and lists the original developers’ cut-offs and probabilities where available. The accompanying discussion notes that, despite the table’s favorable description of LRINEC predictive power, a cited meta-analysis found poor sensitivity for necrotising fasciitis. No scoring system is identified as the preferred choice for FG.

main_conclusion: FG care requires coordinated resuscitation, prompt debridement, antibiotics, reconstruction and follow-up across specialist teams. Mortality remains substantial despite improvement, while decisions about diversion, orchidectomy and adjunctive treatment depend on the individual case; the authors call for more research on long-term quality of life.
narrative_summary:
This non-systematic PubMed review examines the management of Fournier’s gangrene (FG) and the usefulness of prognostic scores. The authors describe FG as a rapidly spreading infection requiring immediate assessment, resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics and urgent removal of necrotic tissue. Historical mortality estimates were 15–40%, whereas a cited meta-analysis reported a mean of 7.3%. Cultures can guide subsequent antimicrobial selection, but imaging should not postpone debridement when FG is clinically evident. A cited study associated debridement delays beyond 14h with increased mortality.

Four FG-specific scores are discussed alongside more general tools. The table reports, at a cut-off of 9, death and survival probabilities of 75% and 78% for FGSI and 94% and 81% for UFGSI, based on their original studies. The authors find no clear consensus on which score should guide practice. They also emphasize repeated wound assessment, possible further debridement and reconstruction tailored to the defect. Evidence for improved mortality with VAC therapy is unclear. Although studies suggest a mortality benefit from adjunctive HBOT, the European Association of Urology (EAU) advises against its use outside clinical trials because the evidence is of low quality. After discharge, follow-up should address treatment-related physical, sexual and psychological difficulties; the authors identify long-term outcomes and quality of life as priorities for further research.

document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: This review outlines predictive scoring systems for Fournier’s gangrene (FG) and offers an evidence-based guide to patient care. Four FG-related tools are discussed: Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotizing Fasciitis, Fournier’s Gangrene Severity Index, Uludag Fournier’s Gangrene Severity Index, and Simplified Fournier’s Gangrene Severity Index; other general tools are also available. The proposed approach spans assessment, resuscitation, investigations, urgent treatment, postoperative care, and long-term follow-up. Care involves resuscitation, surgical debridement, inpatient antibiotic treatment, wound reconstruction, and follow-up, with multidisciplinary expertise needed throughout. Mortality has improved but remains substantial. Further research is needed on individualized care and quality of life after discharge.

document_sections.heading: Plain language summary
document_sections.content: Care for Fournier’s gangrene extends from initial resuscitation and surgical removal of dead tissue through inpatient antibiotics, reconstruction, and long-term follow-up. Each stage requires multidisciplinary expertise. Further work is needed on tailoring care and assessing quality of life after discharge.

document_sections.heading: Introduction
document_sections.content: Jean-Alfred Fournier described FG in 1883 as infectious necrotising fasciitis affecting the external genitalia, perineum, or perianal region. Its high mortality makes it a urological emergency. FG is rare and occurs predominantly in men. Documented risk factors include diabetes mellitus, excess alcohol use, lower socioeconomic status, immunocompromise, and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection. Infection usually begins in an anorectal or genital site and can spread rapidly, causing life-threatening sepsis. Traditional mortality estimates are 15–40%; a recent meta-analysis reported mean mortality of 7.3%. Patients require prompt, aggressive resuscitation and broad-spectrum antibiotics while clinicians obtain a history, examine them, arrange investigations, and discuss care with relevant teams, patients, and families. After the best achievable stabilization, timely, extensive operative debridement remains the standard treatment. Several debridements are usually needed during admission, and some patients need colectomy or urinary diversion. The physiological burden calls for coordinated surgical, medical, nursing, and therapy care. Once debridement is no longer required, plastic surgery may close the wound, sometimes using a substantial skin graft. Evidence on outcomes after discharge is limited; physical and psychological needs warrant attention. The article aims to guide management and review predictive scores available to clinicians.

document_sections.heading: Methods
document_sections.content: The authors conducted a non-systematic PubMed literature review of contemporary FG management, pathogenesis, risk factors, treatments, reconstruction, outcomes, and follow-up. Searches used ‘Fournier’, ‘gangrene’, ‘management’, ‘treatment’, ‘reconstruction’, ‘outcomes’, ‘antibiotic’, and ‘microorganism’. They combined these with ‘scoring’, ‘system’, and ‘index’ to examine the uses and advantages of scoring systems.

document_sections.heading: Pathogenesis
document_sections.content: In Eke’s review of over 1700 cases, sepsis arose chiefly from the anorectum (30–50%), urogenitalia (20–40%), and genital skin (20%); colorectal origins carried a worse prognosis. Frequent sources include perianal, perirectal, and ischiorectal abscesses. Scrotal abscesses and urinary tract infections are also implicated; less common reported causes include trauma, vasectomy, and foreign-body insertion into the penile urethra. FG infection is polymicrobial, often yielding several organisms from one wound. Reported pathogens include Staphylococcus species, Streptococcus species, Escherichia coli, Pseudomonas species, and Bacteroides species; Candida species are the most frequent nonbacterial pathogens. Prevalence differs between studies, making local microbiological guidance and resistance patterns important. Infection produces obliterative endarteritis, inflammation, and oedema. Reduced cutaneous and subcutaneous blood supply causes necrosis and purple-black skin discoloration. Hypoxic tissue supports anaerobes that generate hydrogen and nitrogen; subcutaneous accumulation can produce palpable crepitus. Spread along fascial planes can destroy tissue in the perineum, scrotum, lower abdominal wall, and upper thighs. Spread beneath muscle layers into muscle is uncommon. The testis and epididymis are usually spared because their blood supply has a separate origin.

document_sections.heading: Risk factors
document_sections.content: Reduced host immunity and physiological reserve are principal underlying risks. Diabetes mellitus is the most frequently reported comorbidity, affecting 30–40% of FG patients, and is associated with higher mortality. Sustained hyperglycaemia impairs phagocyte activity, chemotaxis, and cellular adherence; microvascular damage also restricts blood supply and wound healing. FG outcomes vary with the degree of hyperglycaemia, supporting strict glycaemic control during illness. Other reported immune-related risks include immunosuppressive medications, malnutrition, and HIV infection. Huayllani et al. reported hypertension (26%), anaemia (10%), heart failure (6%), and obesity (12%) among FG patients, although their effects on outcomes remain disputed. Multivariate analyses in large studies identified age, renal failure, coagulopathy, and congestive heart failure as significant mortality risk factors.

document_sections.heading: Clinical assessment History and examination
document_sections.content: Because FG can progress rapidly and become fatal, early recognition and vigorous resuscitation are essential. An A–E assessment and indicated resuscitation may need to precede a full history, depending on haemodynamic stability. Symptoms are often nonspecific and can resemble scrotal cellulitis, scrotal abscess, or severe epididymo-orchitis. Local manifestations include scrotal swelling, scrotal or perineal pain, erythema, and skin necrosis; advanced infection may cause fever, vomiting, and altered consciousness. Progression varies but can occur over 3–5days, beginning with increasing discomfort or pain and pruritus. Swelling and skin changes indicate more advanced soft-tissue gangrene. Diabetes mellitus, HIV infection, or immunosuppressive medication should lower the threshold for suspecting FG. Genital and perineal examination is performed with a chaperone. Swelling, erythema, warmth, and tenderness indicate inflammation; the edge of erythema should be marked for comparison at later examinations. Palpable crepitus indicates subcutaneous gas from gas-producing anaerobic infection. Any wound discharge should be sampled for culture. Extension from the genital or perineal area to the thighs or abdominal wall is concerning. Foul-smelling, purple-black skin necrosis is characteristic. PR examination should assess perianal involvement and may reveal a perianal or perirectal abscess as the infectious source.

document_sections.heading: Investigations
document_sections.content: Initial venous tests should include full blood count, urea and electrolytes, C-reactive protein, and clotting profile. A group and save is needed in case blood products are required during emergency care or surgery. Arterial blood gas testing promptly provides haemoglobin, sodium, potassium, and lactate values and assesses acidosis and oxygenation to guide fluids and oxygen. Blood glucose measurement supports glycaemic control. Cultures from blood, urine, wound discharge, and debrided tissue can identify organisms and direct subsequent antibiotics; results are usually interpretable in 72h, when susceptibility patterns permit more targeted treatment. Blood cultures are rarely positive in FG, but positivity is associated with worse outcomes. Urine cultures may be positive when urinary tract infection triggered FG, whereas wound cultures provide the most useful antibiotic guidance. Diagnosis is usually clinical. Obvious or extensive FG should proceed to debridement without an imaging-related delay. Ultrasound (US) and computerised tomography (CT) are the modalities used most often; CT has greater specificity for evaluating disease, can assess the gastrointestinal tract when a colorectal source is suspected, and clarifies anatomy for operative planning, including possible faecal diversion. CT findings include subcutaneous emphysema, fascial thickening, fat stranding, and abscess or fluid collection.

document_sections.heading: Use of scoring systems
document_sections.content: Scores in clinical practice can support diagnosis, treatment decisions, and predictions of morbidity or mortality. Wong et al. created Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotizing Fasciitis (LRINEC) in 2004 from biochemical markers using multivariate logistic regression. At a cut-off of six points, they reported positive and negative predictive values of 92.0% and 96.0%, respectively. LRINEC uses six routinely obtained biochemical markers. Some evidence supports distinguishing necrotising fasciitis from other soft-tissue infections, and some studies suggest seven as a better cut-off. In contrast, a meta-analysis of 23 studies reported poor sensitivity: 68.2% for LRINEC ⩾6 and 40.8% for LRINEC ⩾8. Clinical assessment, with imaging when appropriate, therefore remains necessary. No published study has assessed LRINEC specifically as a diagnostic test for FG; some case studies suggest it may predict FG mortality and mechanical ventilation. In 1995, Laor et al. examined demographic, clinical, laboratory, disease-extent, and debridement data from 30 FG patients and developed Fournier’s Gangrene Severity Index (FGSI) through regression analysis to predict mortality. Unlike LRINEC, FGSI includes temperature, heart rate, and respiratory rate. Affected body-surface percentage and number of debridements were excluded because they did not significantly predict mortality. Other studies have repeatedly validated FGSI for mortality prediction and reported associations with further surgery, longer hospitalization, sepsis, and FG-specific complications, suggesting possible value for morbidity prediction. In 2010, Yilmazlar et al., concerned that FGSI underestimated mortality, analysed a series of 80 patients. Their logistic regression identified disease spread and age as additional significant mortality predictors, leading to Uludag Fournier’s Gangrene Severity Index (UFGSI). At a cut-off of nine points, their reported probability of death was 94% for UFGSI >9 and probability of survival was 81% for UFGSI ⩽9; corresponding published FGSI figures were 75% and 78%. External studies validated UFGSI, and one comparison suggested greater sensitivity (75.0% compared with 58.3%) but lower specificity (84.0% compared with 97.3%) than FGSI. Although FGSI and UFGSI have broad validation, calculating them during rapid deterioration can take time. In Roghmann et al.’s prospective cohort, Charlson Comorbidity Index and Surgical Apgar Score predicted outcomes as well as FG-specific indices while being simpler, more broadly applicable, and better validated. Surgical Apgar Score relies on intraoperative anaesthetic measurements, limiting preoperative use. Lin et al. proposed Simplified Fournier’s Gangrene Severity Index in 2013 using serum creatinine, haematocrit, and serum potassium; it is the quickest and simplest of these FG indices and was reported non-inferior to FGSI and UFGSI. An outcome score should be quick and straightforward, robust to differences between operators, sensitive and specific, and supported by evidence that it affects management. There is no consensus on whether FG scoring systems are useful or which to prefer, nor is it clear whether a high predicted mortality should alter decisions about aggressive resuscitation and debridement. Emerging work examines neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), previously correlated with mortality in sepsis, pneumonia, COVID-19, and cancer. NLR has been reported to predict intensive care admission, mechanical ventilation, and mortality in FG, but routine prognostic use requires more research. Table 1 summarizes the scoring systems’ proposed cut-offs, original authors’ death and survival probabilities, advantages, and disadvantages.

document_sections.heading: Management Initial resuscitation
document_sections.content: Treatment begins during assessment when required and continues through admission. Emergency assessment determines the resuscitation needed. Airway measures and high-flow oxygen can be initiated according to pulse oximetry and arterial blood gas results. Intravenous fluids should begin when shock signs occur, including tachycardia, hypotension, reduced Glasgow Coma Score, low urine output, prolonged capillary refill, and cool extremities. Strict fluid-chart recording of urine output guides infusion rate, while immediately available blood-gas electrolytes inform fluid composition. Blood glucose should be measured and hyperglycaemia corrected because sustained elevation impairs healing and increases morbidity and mortality. Patients with diabetes mellitus may also present with diabetic ketoacidosis, making glucose control imperative. Persistent instability after initial resuscitation warrants contacting intensive care. Blood and urine cultures should be obtained if possible. Broad-spectrum antibiotics should start as soon as possible, ideally after cultures unless sampling would cause substantial delay. Local antimicrobial guidelines should direct selection according to local bacterial patterns. Antibiotics commonly used include metronidazole, penicillin, third-generation cephalosporins, gentamicin, carbapenems, vancomycin, fluoroquinolones, and teicoplanin. Combinations are often necessary, and microbiology advice may be needed. In Becerra et al.’s study of 131 patients, 86% of cases yielded multiple bacteria and 55% yielded both Gram-positive and Gram-negative organisms in the same culture. Candida prevalence in that dataset was 24%, versus 1–5% in comparable studies at other institutions. Those investigators proposed considering empirical antifungals for chronic candiduria, recent intensive care unit admission, diabetes mellitus, or immunocompromise. Blood, urine, and debridement-wound culture findings should prompt review of the antimicrobial regimen.

document_sections.heading: Surgical debridement
document_sections.content: Once initial resuscitation has begun and FG is diagnosed clinically or radiologically, extensive operative debridement should occur as soon as possible. Lin et al. identified 14h as the optimal interval for first debridement and associated longer delays with higher mortality. Early contact with anaesthesia and theatre teams supports prompt intervention. Intensive care should also be notified before surgery because postoperative high-dependency care is common; 17.5–30% of patients require at least single-system support, such as mechanical ventilation or dialysis. A colorectal surgeon’s input is needed when the site or extent of necrosis suggests faecal diversion. Initial testing should include a group and save; packed red cells can be cross-matched when presentation includes anaemia or extensive debridement is anticipated. Surgeons should remove necrotic tissue back to normal fascia and healthy bleeding tissue to halt fascial spread. Operative assessment of disease extent informs decisions about urinary diversion, faecal diversion, orchidectomy, or penectomy. Urinary or faecal diversion is generally indicated when wound contamination is a risk. A urethral catheter achieves urinary diversion in most cases and does not appear to affect FG mortality; suprapubic catheterisation is preferred when penile involvement is extensive. Faecal diversion is considered with perianal or anal sphincter involvement or faecal incontinence, usually through diverting colostomy. If indicated, a stoma should preferably be fashioned during the first debridement because this is associated with better mortality outcomes. Orchidectomy and penectomy are uncommon, reported in 5.6% and 0.2% of cases, respectively. Testicular involvement indicates orchidectomy but is rare because the testes receive blood from the gonadal vessels. Debrided tissue should always be cultured, as these results most often guide antimicrobial treatment. Multiple operations are typical, so the wound remains open after initial debridement under a simple dressing or negative pressure wound therapy such as vacuumassisted closure (VAC) therapy. VAC applies subatmospheric pressure and is described as improving perfusion and inflammatory-cell migration to support granulation. It is associated with less frequent dressing changes, better pain control, and greater mobility, but a mortality benefit is not clearly established. Some evidence suggests better wound closure at a 10-week postoperative interval. No large-scale randomized trial has compared VAC therapy with simple wound closure, limiting conclusions.

document_sections.heading: Reconstructive techniques
document_sections.content: Plastic surgery review should be arranged postoperatively to plan definitive closure. Options include secondary intention, delayed primary closure, loose wound approximation, skin flap, and skin graft. Testicular placement in a thigh pocket is occasionally used temporarily before reconstruction or as permanent coverage. Extensive debridement can make reconstruction difficult; no standard preferred method exists, so the approach is tailored to each patient. Secondary intention may suit relatively small wounds, especially those limited to the scrotum. Healing takes longer and cosmetic control is reduced, but avoiding loose approximation can reduce the risk of worsening or spreading infection. Scrotal advancement flaps offer better appearance for small scrotal wounds but risk flap failure and necrosis. They should be avoided for larger defects because greater closure tension increases failure risk. Split-thickness skin grafting and thigh flaps can cover larger defects; recognized complications include graft loss, infection, scarring, adhesions, dehiscence, unacceptable appearance, and reduced sensation. Extensive perianal debridement can leave dead space that undermines antimicrobial efficacy and reconstruction through bacterial colonisation and chronic inflammation. In a retrospective comparison, Ismayilzade et al. found significantly fewer revisions for wound dehiscence and significantly shorter hospital stays after pedicled gracilis muscle flap surgery to fill dead space than when no specific dead-space procedure was used. That study was small (n =22) and retrospective, so further research would be valuable.

document_sections.heading: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy
document_sections.content: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) is used for several critical conditions, including necrotising soft-tissue infection, carbon monoxide poisoning, traumatic ischaemia, radiation-related tissue injury, and thermal burns. In these conditions, hypoxia can cause ischaemia and necrosis that favour anaerobic growth. Proposed wound-healing effects of HBOT involve controlled reactive oxygen and nitrogen species generation, increased growth-factor production, and neovascularisation. A direct effect against anaerobes and reduced endotoxin activity in highly oxygenated tissue have also been proposed. Evidence suggests significantly lower mortality when HBOT supplements debridement and antibiotics, although its use depends on available facilities and expertise. Nevertheless, European Association of Urology (EAU) guidelines advise against HBOT outside clinical trials because the existing evidence is low quality.

document_sections.heading: Outcomes and follow-up
document_sections.content: FG and repeated procedures substantially tax patients’ physiological reserve and require several specialist teams. Little guidance defines standardized long-term care or follow-up. Possible lasting problems include reduced physical role functioning, sexual dysfunction, painful or uncomfortable scars, faecal or urinary incontinence, and psychological dysfunction. Sorensen reported that, at discharge, 23% of patients needed ‘home health care’ and 6% needed a ‘skilled nursing facility’. Follow-up should reflect each patient’s inpatient treatments and operations. After diverting colostomy, this includes stoma nursing and colorectal outpatient review to discuss possible reversal and bowel anastomosis. The article states that rehabilitation after discharge should include consideration of reconstructive surgery and other therapies, such as intermittent hyperbaric oxygen therapy with multiparameter diagnostic monitoring. It notes that sepsis develops in over 40% of FG patients and is reflected in high 1- and 5-year mortality.

document_sections.heading: Conclusion
document_sections.content: FG care comprises initial resuscitation, debridement, inpatient antibiotic treatment, reconstruction, and long-term follow-up; every stage is important and depends on multidisciplinary expertise. Mortality has fallen from historical levels but remains substantial. Although more aspects of care are becoming standardized, decisions about diverting stomas, orchidectomy, and adjuncts such as hyperbaric oxygen therapy remain individualized and depend on the treating surgical teams’ experience. Additional research into long-term outcomes is needed to improve quality of life after discharge.
